paragraphs.heading: Space and time as one
paragraphs.text: Minkowski spacetime, often just called Minkowski space, is the main mathematical picture of space and time when gravity is left out. It joins space and time into a single model with four dimensions. In it, the spacetime interval separating two events comes out the same no matter which inertial frame records them. It is tied closely to Einstein's special and general relativity, and it is the usual mathematical form in which special relativity is written down.

paragraphs.heading: Time is treated differently
paragraphs.text: Observers moving relative to each other can disagree on the separate amounts of space and time between two events, because of length contraction and time dilation. Yet they all agree on the combined interval. Minkowski space also differs from an ordinary four-dimensional space in one key way: it handles time differently from the three space directions. There is a second, stranger difference. In everyday Euclidean space two different points always lie some distance apart, but here two different events can have an interval of zero, which happens when one sits on the light cone of the other.

paragraphs.heading: Sorting directions
paragraphs.text: Write a four-dimensional vector as v = (ct, x, y, z) = (ct, r), where c is the universal speed limit, t is time and x, y, z are positions in space. The vector is sorted by the sign of c²t² − r². When c²t² > r² the vector is called timelike; when c²t² < r² it is called spacelike; when the two are equal it is null, or lightlike. Every frame linked by a Lorentz transformation sorts the vector the same way, since the interval does not change under such a transformation.

paragraphs.heading: Lorentz and Poincaré
paragraphs.text: The story starts in the 1890s, when Hendrik Lorentz built theories of electrodynamics around an aether, a medium thought to fill all of space. From 1892 to 1904 he used the transformations now named after him as mathematical aids. Minkowski knew the work of Henri Poincaré well, especially a 1905 paper. There Poincaré treated time as an imaginary fourth coordinate, ict, so that Lorentz transformations looked like ordinary rotations in four dimensions. He also picked out quantities that stay fixed under that rotation, such as x² + y² + z² − t².

paragraphs.heading: Minkowski's 1908 step
paragraphs.text: Minkowski developed these ideas in a 1908 paper in German on the basic equations of electromagnetism in moving bodies. He brought tensors into the physics and rewrote Maxwell's equations as a symmetric set in the four variables x, y, z and ict. He showed that these equations keep their form under a Lorentz transformation. From this he concluded that time and space deserve equal treatment, with events taking place in one unified four-dimensional continuum. In a lecture he declared that space alone and time alone would fade into shadows, and only a union of the two would stay real.

paragraphs.heading: Why it mattered
paragraphs.text: The rest of that lecture leaned on mathematics, favouring four-vectors for positions and velocities. It introduced the Minkowski diagram, which Minkowski used to explain ideas such as proper time and length contraction. The upshot was to treat the mathematics as revealing something real about nature, not just as a handy tool. The four-vector way of describing spacetime went on to become the standard language of relativity. Einstein was not keen at first, though: Minkowski's picture left out gravity, which Einstein knew had to be included.
